revise.summary: I revised content/lessons/06-prototype.md against the 1.3.1 prototype, LOGIC.md, UI.md, handoff, ask-matt and PHASE-BOUNDARIES files. The capture now matches rule 6 everywhere: in the Scene the user asks for the settled details, the winner is folded into the real code, and the body says the Skill records little more than the verdict and question unless you ask (as issue #1306 describes). The detour section now names /grill-with-docs and /to-tickets, says why the detour passes the "something must travel" test (a side task forked off mid-phase), explains how to open a fresh session, and gives the phase-boundary list with Continue's real conditions and ask-matt's "don't push on near the Smart zone" limit. The Try block now works from zero on PowerShell and macOS: one command per line, git init -b main, the author-identity fix, steps in the right order, a committed DECISION.md, and checks a non-coder can do. The Site story is rebuilt only from repo facts: the old journal Lesson at d21fc2c, commit 8cdcfa1 (read through the GitHub API, and it diverged from main), and the issue 03 and 06 notes. All session-log facts are cut (205k tokens, "c lets go with c", the long-form command, "same session"). In the questions, scenario-detour became scenario-detour-return, which tests the return trip. Body examples were swapped for fresh ones, the wording tells are gone, and every right answer is shorter than at least one wrong option by both measures.

quiz.where: Final test, spot-handoff-misuse, lines 383-393: "with plenty of room left in the session: same folder, same tool" / [x] "nothing had to travel"
quiz.problem: This tests recall, not transfer, and the wording gives the answer away. The prompt restates the Lesson's own sentence about going from planning to building and lists the 'no travel' tests in advance (same folder, same tool, room left). The right option then repeats the Lesson's catchphrase 'travel', which no wrong option uses. Option d ('should have prototyped') is a weak distractor, because nothing in the scenario points to an open question.
quiz.evidence: Line 191: "Going from planning straight to building, in the same place, with room left? Carry on: the build wants your reasoning word for word." The 'travel' phrase also appears at line 183 ("a file that travels"), line 187 ("only if something must travel"), line 280 ("when nothing has to travel") and line 306 ("Nothing has to travel"). The answer key itself is correct: PHASE-BOUNDARIES.md:21 says grilling to implementation is "the standard yes" for Continue.
quiz.fix: Prompt: "Priya grilled a one-ticket change to her band's gig-listing site, and the session is still well inside the Smart zone. She types `/handoff`, starts a fresh session with the file and builds the change there. Spot the mistake." Options: [x] "She should have built it in the session that did the grilling." > "Right. The build wants the grilling word for word, and there was room. `/handoff` buys a file that travels, and nothing was going anywhere." / [ ] "She should have typed `/clear` instead, so the build starts clean." > "Clearing throws away the decisions the build needs. The fix is not to leave the session at all." / [ ] "She should have asked the agent to run `/handoff` for her." > "`/handoff` is user-invoked, so only you can start it. And here it wasn't needed anyway." / [ ] "She should have run `/compact` first, so the build starts from a summary." > "There was room left, so there was nothing to shrink. Carrying on comes first in the checklist and keeps the grilling word for word."

quiz.where: Final test, spot-colour-variants, lines 359-369: [x] "The variants differ in styling, not structure."
quiz.problem: Wording tell. All three wrong options are remedies phrased as 'should have' or 'needed' ("Sam should have asked…", "The variants needed tests…", "They should have been built…"). The right option alone is a present-tense diagnosis, and at 46 characters it is far shorter than the others (52-82). A reader can pick it on form alone.
quiz.evidence: Option lengths measured from the file: a 82 chars, b (right) 46, c 52, d 52. The answer key is correct: UI.md:54 says "Variants must be **structurally different**… not just different colours".
quiz.fix: Make all four options diagnoses of about the same length: [ ] "There were too few variants for one of them to come out different." / [x] "All three share one layout and differ only in styling." / [ ] "The variants weren't tested before Sam looked at them." / [ ] "The variants weren't put on a separate new route of their own." Keep the existing feedback lines, reworded to match.

quiz.evidence: 'What it settled' appears in goal line 16 ("the verdict and what it settled on the ticket"), line 145 ("ask for what it settled"), line 151 ("ask for what the winner settled"), Common mistakes line 279 ("Recording a winner but not what it settled") and Cheat sheet line 304. The right option and option b are both 14 words, the joint longest.
quiz.fix: [ ] "They should have merged C's prototype code, so the agent could reuse it." > "Prototype code skips tests and error handling, so it's rewritten, never merged. The gap was in what the ticket recorded." / [ ] keep b / [ ] "They should have put the verdict in a commit message instead of the ticket." > "A commit message is a fine home for the verdict, but it would still only say C. Where it was written wasn't the gap." / [x] "They should have recorded C's details on the ticket, not just its letter." > "Right. Write down the question and the details C settled (field order, help text), with a pointer to the `prototype/<name>` branch."

(line 74), and Checkpoint winner-goes-where, option b feedback "Parking it too means rebuilding checked rules from memory." (line 122), with option a "The rules block moves into the real code" (line 119)

In 1.3.1 the whole prototype is committed to the branch, and the logic file stays runnable there because it is one self-contained file. That needs the rules block inside it. Option b's real error is not lifting the rules into the code, not parking them.

Line 119 (option a): "The rules block is copied into the real code; the whole page goes onto a `prototype/<name>` branch." accuracy.where: Six rules, capture bullet "The prototype goes onto a branch named `prototype/<name>`" (line 112); same claim in goals (line 16) and the cheat sheet (line 304)
accuracy.problem: This is written as if the Skill names the branch. The 1.3.1 Skill files the agent actually loads say only "a throwaway branch". The `prototype/<name>` pattern comes from ask-matt and the CHANGELOG, so the agent may pick a different name unless you ask. The Try it handles this by naming the branch, but the body doesn't say why.
accuracy.evidence: SKILL.md:26: "commit it to a throwaway branch, out of main". UI.md:100: "move the rest onto the throwaway branch". The pattern appears only in ask-matt/SKILL.md:87 ("on a `prototype/<name>` branch out of main") and CHANGELOG.md:118.
accuracy.fix: "**The prototype goes onto a branch of its own** that is never merged (its commits never join `main`). Matt names it `prototype/<name>`; the Skill itself just says a throwaway branch, so say the name you want, as the Try it does."

accuracy.where: The idea, "Since version 1.2.0 of Matt's Skills, the answer goes into the real code and the prototype is parked in Git" (line 38)
accuracy.problem: This implies that folding the answer into the real code also started in 1.2.0. Only keeping the prototype is new. The logic module already lifted into the real code before 1.2.0.
accuracy.evidence: CHANGELOG.md:116 (1.2.0, #763): "The portable pure-logic module still lifts into the real code; the HTML shell is the throwaway." CHANGELOG.md:118: "Throwaway no longer means deleted."
accuracy.fix: "It doesn't mean deleted. The answer always went into the real code; since version 1.2.0 of Matt's Skills, the prototype is also kept, parked in Git (the tool that records a project's history) as evidence."

reader.where: The detour: /handoff out and back: "One limit sits over the list: near the edge of the Smart zone, don't push on; `/compact` at the next boundary.", line 191
reader.problem: Because the limit is placed "over the list", it overrides steps 2 to 4. A reader near the edge whose context is disposable gets two answers: `/clear` from step 2 and `/compact` from the limit. The same clash happens for a side task that has to travel. The source tree has no such override. Its "don't push on" line covers the planning window and only rules out carrying on.
reader.evidence: ~/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/mattpocock-skills/1.3.1/skills/engineering/ask-matt/PHASE-BOUNDARIES.md:19 says "Work top to bottom at the boundary. The first **yes** wins." Line 23 of the same file says to `/clear` when the context is disposable. ask-matt/SKILL.md:40 says "If a session approaches it before `/to-tickets`, don't push on degraded; `/compact` at the nearest phase boundary". That rule is scoped to steps 1–3 of the Main flow.
reader.fix: "One limit sits over step 1: near the edge of the Smart zone, don't carry on, even when the next step wants this conversation word for word. Go on down the list. For a planning session whose context you still need, it lands on `/compact`."

reader.where: Try it yourself, Stretch: "After step 6, type `/handoff prototype the late-fee rules in a fresh session and report back`" … "`/handoff back to the planning session`", line 270
reader.problem: The stretch runs the detour the wrong way round. After step 6, the prototype has already been built in window one. Its tokens are already there, and window one was never a planning session. This contradicts the detour section, where the point is that "None of the prototype's tokens ever landed here".
